newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch money market closely watching DTC programme.
newsitem.headline: Dutch money market closely watching DTC programme.

text.p: The short-term borrowing programme of the Dutch government, which has put upward pressure on money market rates in recent weeks, will be closely monitored when funding figures are updated on Tuesday, analysts said.

They said the Agency of the Ministry of Finance initially received a poor reception last month when it stepped up its issuance of Dutch Treasury Certificates (DTCs), putting the spotlight on how much extra the agency has to raise this year.
They estimate the remaining issuance programme in 1996 at between six billion and nine billion guilders.
"It's very interesting to look at DTCs at the moment because they're disturbing the market quite heavily," said ABN AMRO Hoare Govett senior bond strategist Gerlof de Vrij.
The Agency will announce on Tuesday the total outstanding in DTCS, which are short-term funding instruments, including the amount raised last week.
The agency, the government's debt raising arm, is relying on DTCs to meet its remaining funding needs this year because it plans no new bond issues in 1996.
Between October 1 and October 28, it issued 4.5 billion guilders of DTCs, maturing in January, February and March 1997.

Analysts said a combination of this extra supply, comments from Bundesbank officials ruling out lower German interest rates and rumours of a hike in the Dutch special advances rate pushed Dutch short term interest rates sharply higher last month.
The rates on the new DTC issues peaked above 2.90 percent last week from below 2.80 percent several weeks earlier as the agency was forced to raise rates to attract buyers, they said.
"It's a big issue. Maybe not everbody was waiting for so much money," said De Vrij.
He said it also represented a structural shift in funding by the agency, which previously relied more heavily on bonds.
"A lot of people expected it to be hard for the (agency) to place them," he said, adding however that he expected 10-15 billion guilders of DTCs to be outstanding at the end of 1996.
One money market dealer said the agency had attracted a lot of attention by raising rates on DTCs each day in succession when it started stepping up issuance in early October.
"The market was a little bit unsure about that," he said, adding however that it finally tempted buyers with higher rates and made progress in moving toward its funding target.
"I would say the pressure is off. We will know more about it tomorrow morning," he said.
But he said part of the problem for the agency was a shortage of liquidity in the money market last week when the Dutch central bank's advances pact fell short of expectations.
IRIS strategist Leon Cornellisen said he expected another 9.0 billion guilders of DTCs to be issued before the end of this year, although this would depend on the final budget deficit.
"At the start they had some problems. Not everybody was subscribing, but they made it more attractive," he said.
He also said he doubted that money market rates would continue to rise or that the yield gap to Germany would keep narrowing.
-- Garry West, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
